questions.question: Describe different types of families and explain how family structures have changed in the UK.

points.text: Family types: nuclear (two-generation, most common), extended (multi-generation, declining), reconstituted (step-families, 10%), lone-parent (25%, mostly female-headed), same-sex (increasing since 2014 marriage equality). Changes: decline of nuclear, rise of cohabitation, more lone-parent and same-sex families, increase in childless couples, later marriage and childbearing.

questions.question: Evaluate the view that the nuclear family is the best family type for society.

points.text: Functionalists argue the nuclear family is best: it performs essential functions (Murdock: sexual, reproductive, economic, educational) and is suited to industrial society (Parsons: geographically mobile). However: this ignores family diversity, assumes all nuclear families are functional (domestic violence, abuse), and pathologises other family types. Feminists argue the nuclear family oppresses

questions.question: Assess the causes and consequences of increasing family diversity.

points.text: Causes of diversity: secularisation (less religious influence on family life), changing gender roles (women's economic independence), easier divorce (1969 Divorce Reform Act), contraception (decoupling sex from reproduction), welfare state (financial support for lone parents). Consequences: greater individual freedom but also potential instability. New Right sees diversity as causing social proble

markScheme.exemplarAnswer: A grade 9 response will: define family diversity and describe changes (decline of nuclear, rise of cohabitation, lone-parent, same-sex); present positive impacts (individual freedom, women's independence, acceptance of difference, reduced stigma); present negative impacts (New Right: instability, welfare dependency, fatherless families); evaluate using evidence (most children in lone-parent families do well; diversity reflects choice not decline); conclude: family diversity is largely positive - it reflects greater individual freedom and equality, and there is no evidence that non-nuclear families are inherently worse. The quality of relationships matters more than family structure.
